Exam Guide

Claude Certified Associate - Foundations

Version 1.0  ·  Effective July 2026  ·  Exam code: CCAO-F  ·  This guide is subject to change without notice.

1. About This Certification

The Claude Certi fi ed Associate  -  Foundations certi fi cation validates that an individual can apply Claude to complete business and productivity tasks with minimal guidance. This includes using built-in platform features, capabilities, and tools to streamline work fl ows; identifying opportunities to improve processes with Claude; selecting approaches that balance quality, ef fi ciency, and cost; and recognizing limitations and escalating more complex or technical work to Claude Architects and Developers.

1. About This Certification

It is intended for professionals who use Claude as a productivity tool in roles such as operations, marketing, project management, education, and communications. This guide is the authoritative reference for candidates preparing to sit the exam; it describes the credential's purpose, audience, exam format and blueprint, scoring, policies, and rules of conduct. Read it in full before scheduling.

concepts.title: Minimally Qualified Candidate (MQC) Profile
concepts.summary: The MQC is a professional who uses Claude as a core productivity tool, applying it to improve efficiency and outcomes through foundational and applied knowledge.

grounding.text:
4. Minimally Qualified Candidate Profile

The exam is targeted at the minimally quali fi ed candidate (MQC): a professional who uses Claude as a core productivity tool and can apply it effectively within real-world work fl ows to improve ef fi ciency, quality, and outcomes. The MQC has foundational, applied knowledge of Claude's capabilities, including prompt structuring, task orchestration, and familiarity with features such as Projects, Artifacts, and work fl ow-based interactions, and moves beyond basic question-and-answer usage to process reimagination, task automation, and project development.

4. Minimally Qualified Candidate Profile

The MQC is aware of organizational context: how Claude creates value, where adoption risks exist, and how to align usage with business needs and responsible-AI practices. They have regular, hands-on experience using Claude in a professional setting and can independently complete common productivity and work fl ow tasks on the platform.

Recommended experience

- Regular, hands-on experience using Claude in a professional setting
- A foundational understanding of structured problem-solving, work fl ow design, and digital tool usage

Claude Certification Program

- Experience in roles such as business analyst, project manager, operations lead, marketing/communications/HR/education professional, consultant, or knowledge worker
- A practical understanding of AI limitations, including hallucinations, context constraints, and data sensitivity

concepts.title: Prompting and Task Execution
concepts.summary: This domain covers creating effective prompts, using task decomposition for complex requests, iterating prompts for quality improvement, and adapting strategies based on the task type.

grounding.text:
Domain 1: Prompting and Task Execution (14%)

- Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
- Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
- Iterate prompts to improve output quality
- Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)

Domain 2: Output Evaluation and Validation (21%)

- Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
- Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
- Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
- Determine when human review or additional veri fi cation is required
- Edit, adapt, re fi ne, and compare outputs for the intended audience
- Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)

Domain 3: Product and Model Selection (12%)

- Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
- Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
- Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
- Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)

Domain 4: Work fl ow Integration and Solution Design (16%)

- Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
- Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
- Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
- Integrate Claude into existing work fl ows to augment or redesign them

concepts.title: Exam Scoring Methodology
concepts.summary: The Claude Certified Associate exam is criterion-referenced, meaning performance is measured against a fixed standard, not against other test-takers.

grounding.text:
Sample 1 · Domain 2  -  Output Evaluation and Validation

- A. Send it as-is, since Claude expressed high con fi dence.
- B. Verify the cited subsection against the of fi cial regulation text before sharing.
- C. Ask Claude to rate its own con fi dence and send it if the rating is high.
- D. Reword the summary to sound more formal, then send it.

Sample 2 · Domain 3  -  Product and Model Selection

An associate needs to generate a high volume of short customer-reply drafts where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning. Which choice best  fi ts the task?

Sample 2 · Domain 3  -  Product and Model Selection

- A. Use the most capable, highest-cost model for every reply to maximize quality.

Claude Certification Program

- B. Use a faster, lower-cost model suited to straightforward, high-volume tasks.
- C. Disable all product features to reduce cost.
- D. Switch to a different AI platform.

Sample 3 · Domain 6  -  Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

A project manager wants to upload a spreadsheet containing customer names and account numbers so Claude can analyze trends. Organizational policy restricts sharing regulated personal data. What is the most appropriate action?

10. Registration and Scheduling

1. Go to the certi fi cation page for your exam on the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the exam details.
2. Download the Exam Guide and review the Certi fi cation Terms and Conditions and the Certi fi cation Exam Policy before registering.
3. Register for the exam and complete checkout. The fee shown at checkout re fl ects any discount that applies to your partner tier.
4. Follow the con fi rmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account, then sign in to schedule your exam session.
5. Choose an available date and select either online proctoring or a Pearson test center. The exam is delivered by Pearson VUE.
6. You may cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment. Changes made within 24 hours forfeit the exam fee.

Identi fi cation

On exam day you must present a valid, unexpired, government-issued photo identi fi cation. The name on your ID must match the name on your registration exactly. If you need to correct the name on your registration, contact certi fi cations-support@anthropic.com before scheduling your exam.

Accommodations

Reasonable accommodations are available for candidates with documented disabilities or needs, in accordance with applicable law. Accommodations must be requested and approved by Pearson VUE before you schedule your exam. Do not schedule your appointment until your request has been approved. concepts.title: Prompting as a Professional Skill
concepts.summary: Prompting is treated as a professional skill in the Foundations exam, requiring the translation of real-world business or technical goals into clear, well-scoped requests.

grounding.text:
# Create Effective Prompts for Business and Technical Tasks

A prompt is the instruction you give Claude, and the quality of that instruction is the single biggest lever you control over the quality of the result. The Foundations exam treats prompting as a professional skill: it rewards candidates who can translate a real business or technical goal into a clear, well-scoped request, and it penalizes the habit of typing a vague one-liner and hoping for the best.


##### The core mental model

Anthropic's own guidance frames it simply: treat Claude like a brilliant but brand-new colleague who is capable but has no context on your norms, your audience, or your definition of "good." A new hire who is handed "make me a dashboard" will guess; a new hire who is told what the dashboard is for, who will read it, and what it must contain will deliver something usable. The same is true of Claude. The more precisely you explain what you want, the closer the first draft lands.

A useful test comes straight from the docs: show your prompt to a person who lacks context and ask them to follow it. If they would be confused, Claude will be too. That "confused colleague" check is exactly the kind of judgment the exam is probing.


##### The building blocks of a strong prompt

Effective prompts combine several ingredients. You rarely need all of them, but knowing each one lets you choose deliberately.

**Clarity and explicit instructions.** Be specific and direct about what you want. "Summarize

concepts.title: Business Framing
concepts.summary: Business tasks emphasize audience, purpose, and tone, requiring prompts to specify who the stakeholders are, the goal, and the desired style.

grounding.text:
##### Business framing versus technical framing

The exam candidate is a business professional, and prompts for business tasks tend to emphasize *audience, purpose, and tone*. A prompt to draft a stakeholder update should name who the stakeholders are, what decision the update supports, how formal it should read, and what length fits the channel. The success criteria are persuasion, clarity, and appropriateness, so the prompt should encode those.

Technical tasks — analyzing a spreadsheet, structuring data, outlining a process, drafting documentation — tend to emphasize *precision, correctness, and structure*. Here you lean harder on explicit steps, exact output formats, and instructions to ground the answer in provided material. At the Foundations altitude this still means natural-language prompting in the product, not code: you are asking Claude to reason over documents or data you supply, and you are specifying the structure of the answer, not writing an API call.

Both framings share the same skeleton — clarity, context, format, constraints — but weight the ingredients differently.


##### A worked mini-example

Weak: "Write a product launch announcement."

Strong: "You are our product marketing lead. Write a launch announcement email for our existing small-business customers announcing a new invoicing feature. Goal: drive them to try it this week. concepts.title: Task Decomposition
concepts.summary: Task decomposition is the process of breaking a large, complex request into smaller, ordered sub-tasks to ensure each part receives focused attention from the model.

grounding.text:
# Apply Task Decomposition Techniques to Structure Complex Requests

When a request is large or has several moving parts, cramming it into a single prompt usually produces a mediocre result: Claude may skip a step, blur two requirements together, or lose the thread halfway through. Task decomposition is the discipline of breaking a big ask into smaller, ordered sub-tasks so each one gets focused attention. The Foundations exam treats this as a judgment skill — knowing *when* a task needs to be broken up, and *how* to sequence the pieces.


##### Why decomposition works

Anthropic's guidance is direct about the failure mode: when a single prompt tries to juggle too many elements, the model can overlook or mishandle parts of the task. Splitting the work into manageable steps raises accuracy and makes the process easier to follow and fix. If something goes wrong, you can see which step produced the problem instead of re-running one giant, opaque request.

There is a human parallel that maps cleanly onto the exam's business framing. You would not hand a new analyst "produce our quarterly board deck" as one instruction. You would say: pull the numbers, then interpret the trends, then draft the narrative, then design the slides. Each hand-off has a checkpoint. Decomposition gives Claude the same scaffolding and gives you the same checkpoints.


##### When to decompose (and when not to)

Not every task needs breaking down. A short, single-purpose request — "rewrite this paragraph to

concepts.title: Step-by-step prompting
concepts.summary: This technique involves asking the AI to complete a task by explicitly listing sequential, numbered stages within a single prompt to ensure the model addresses each part in order.

grounding.text:
##### The core techniques

**Step-by-step within one prompt.** The lightest form of decomposition is asking Claude to work through a task in explicit, numbered stages inside a single request: "First, list the key risks in this contract. Second, rank them by severity. Third, recommend a mitigation for the top three." Ordering the instructions as sequential steps — the docs recommend numbered lists when order or completeness matters — pushes Claude to address each in turn rather than blending them. This is enough for many everyday tasks.

**Prompt chaining across turns.** For heavier work, treat each sub-task as its own turn and feed the output of one into the next. A canonical business chain is *Research → Outline → Draft → Edit → Format*. You review the research before you approve the outline; you approve the outline before Claude drafts. Because you inspect each intermediate result, errors are caught early instead of propagating into a finished-but-flawed deliverable. Anthropic notes that explicit chaining is especially valuable exactly when you want to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline.

**The self-correction chain.** A particularly powerful pattern is *generate → review → refine*: have Claude produce a draft, then in a fresh step ask it to critique that draft against specific criteria, then have it revise based on the critique. ##### The core techniques

concepts.title: Prompting Pitfalls
concepts.summary: Common errors in prompt engineering include over-decomposing simple tasks, skipping intermediate review checkpoints, losing context across conversational turns, and drawing conclusions before sufficient evidence is presented.

grounding.text:
##### Common pitfalls

- **Over-decomposing trivial tasks**, adding turns and overhead where a single clear prompt would do.
- **Skipping the checkpoints** — chaining only helps if you actually review the intermediate output before moving on; blindly passing it forward re-introduces the errors you were trying to catch.
- **Losing context between turns.** When you chain, make sure each step carries forward what it needs; do not assume Claude remembers an instruction you gave three turns ago unless it is still in view.
- **Sequencing conclusions before evidence**, which produces confident answers unsupported by the source material.

Decomposition, done with judgment, is what turns a sprawling request into a controllable, verifiable process — and knowing when to reach for it is exactly what the exam is checking.

concepts.summary: Prompt engineering should be treated as an empirical loop: critically read the output, diagnose shortcomings, adjust the prompt, and iterate until the desired result is achieved.

grounding.text:
# Iterate Prompts to Improve Output Quality

Very few prompts land perfectly on the first try, and the exam does not expect them to. What it expects is that you treat prompting as a loop: read the output critically, diagnose what fell short, adjust the prompt, and try again. The skill being tested is not writing one magic prompt but knowing how to close the gap between what you got and what you needed.


##### Iteration is the normal workflow, not a failure

Anthropic frames prompt engineering as inherently empirical: you start with a first draft, test it against your success criteria, and refine. The corollary is that a disappointing first answer is data, not a dead end. The professional move is to ask "what specifically is wrong, and which lever fixes it?" rather than either accepting a weak result or scrapping Claude entirely.

This also means you should have a rough idea of "good" before you start. If you cannot say what a successful output looks like — the audience, the format, the must-haves — you cannot tell whether iteration is helping. Defining success criteria first is what makes the loop measurable.


##### Diagnosing a weak output

Before changing anything, pinpoint the failure. Different weaknesses call for different fixes, and guessing wastes turns. Common diagnoses and their remedies:

- **Wrong format or structure** (a wall of text when you wanted a table; bullets when you wanted prose). Fix: state the format explicitly, and tell Claude what to do rather than

concepts.title: Iterative Refinement Strategies
concepts.summary: There are two primary ways to iterate on a prompt: using follow-up turns for conversational adjustments or editing the original prompt for reusable constraints.

grounding.text:
##### Refine in the prompt or in a follow-up turn?

You have two ways to iterate, and choosing well matters.

**Follow-up turns** are fast and conversational: "Good, but make it half the length and add a line about pricing." Because Claude keeps the conversation in view, you can steer incrementally without rewriting everything. This is ideal for polishing a specific output and for exploratory back-and-forth where you are discovering what you want as you go.

**Editing the original prompt** is the better move when you have learned something reusable — a format requirement or a constraint you will want *every* time, or when the conversation has accumulated so many patches that it has become messy and self-contradictory. Folding the lessons back into a clean, improved prompt gives you a repeatable starting point rather than a fragile thread you cannot reproduce. A common pattern: iterate via follow-ups to discover the right instructions, then consolidate those instructions into one solid prompt (or a saved Project instruction) for reuse.

The tempting-but-wrong habit is to keep bolting correction after correction onto an increasingly tangled conversation. Past a point, the accumulated contradictions confuse rather than clarify; starting fresh with a cleaned-up prompt is faster and more reliable.

A compact worked example. First attempt: "Write a summary of this policy document." The result is a generic five-paragraph essay. Diagnosis: too lon

concepts.title: Prompting Strategy Adaptation
concepts.summary: Effective prompting requires tailoring instructions to the specific task type—such as analysis, research, drafting, or brainstorming—because each task has a unique goal and failure mode.

grounding.text:
# Adapt Prompting Strategies Based on Task Type

Good prompting is not one fixed recipe. The instructions that produce a sharp analysis are different from the ones that produce a lively brainstorm, and asking for the wrong thing wastes the interaction. The Foundations exam tests whether you can recognize the *type* of task in front of you — analysis, research, drafting, or brainstorming — and shape the prompt to match. Each task type has a different goal, a different failure mode, and therefore a different set of things worth asking for.


##### Why task type changes the prompt

Every prompt encodes an implicit definition of success. For an analysis the success is *accuracy and defensible reasoning*; for a brainstorm it is *quantity and range*. If you prompt a brainstorm the way you prompt an analysis — demanding one correct, well-justified answer — you will strangle the creativity you wanted. If you prompt an analysis the way you prompt a brainstorm — "give me lots of ideas" — you will get breadth where you needed rigor. Naming the task type first tells you which levers (grounding, structure, tone, divergence) to pull.


##### Analysis

Analytical tasks — interpreting a dataset, reviewing a contract, evaluating options against criteria — live or die on being grounded and structured. The overriding risk is a confident answer that is not actually supported by the material.

What to ask for:

- **Ground the work in the source.** Have Claude quote or cite the specific passages o

concepts.title: Drafting Tasks
concepts.summary: Drafting involves producing polished output like emails or reports, where the key differentiators are audience fit, tone, and format.

grounding.text:
##### Drafting

Drafting tasks — emails, memos, reports, announcements, documentation — are about producing polished output in a specific voice for a specific reader. Correctness still matters, but the differentiator is *audience fit, tone, and format*.

What to ask for:

- **Name the audience and purpose.** Who reads this, and what should they think, feel, or do afterward? A note meant to reassure a nervous client reads nothing like one meant to prompt a fast decision.
- **Set tone and length explicitly**, matched to the channel — a Slack message, a formal report, and a customer email have different registers and different lengths.
- **Specify the format**, and prefer telling Claude what to do over what to avoid ("write in flowing prose paragraphs" rather than "no bullet points").
- **Show a model when you have one.** A past deliverable that hit the mark is often the fastest way to lock in house style — that is few-shot prompting applied to writing.

Drafting is also where iteration pays off most: get a first version, then refine tone and length through follow-up turns. And it is where data-sensitivity discipline applies — anonymize regulated personal information before uploading source material, rather than relying on an instruction to "not retain" it.


##### Brainstorming

Brainstorming inverts the priorities. Here you want *volume, variety, and unexpected angles*, and premature judgment is the enemy. Over-constraining the prompt is the classic mistake.

What to ask for:

concepts.title: Output Evaluation Principles
concepts.summary: Evaluating Claude-generated outputs requires checking two distinct criteria: accuracy (is it true and consistent?) and completeness (did it answer the entire request?).

grounding.text:
# Evaluate Claude-Generated Outputs for Accuracy and Completeness

Output Evaluation and Validation is the heaviest domain on the Claude Certified Associate – Foundations exam, and this is its foundation: before you use, forward, or act on anything Claude produces, you check whether it is both *correct* and *complete*. The exam rewards the habit of treating a Claude response as a draft to be verified, not an answer to be trusted.


##### Two separate questions: accuracy and completeness

A response can be accurate but incomplete, or complete but wrong. Strong evaluation separates the two.

**Accuracy** asks: is what Claude said actually true and internally consistent? Are the facts, figures, names, dates, and quotes correct? Do the conclusions follow from the stated evidence?

**Completeness** asks: did Claude answer the *whole* request? A prompt like "Summarize this contract and flag any termination and liability clauses" contains three deliverables — a summary, termination clauses, and liability clauses. A polished summary that silently ignores liability is a failure, even if every word of the summary is true. The most common evaluation miss is not a false statement; it is a quietly dropped part of the ask.


##### A practical evaluation routine

1. **Restate the ask as a checklist.** List every explicit deliverable and every implicit constraint (audience, length, format, tone, scope). Then confirm the output satisfies each item. This is the single most reliable way to catc

concepts.summary: Accuracy concerns the factual correctness and internal consistency of the content, while completeness ensures all parts of the original prompt have been addressed.

##### Define what "good" means before you judge

Anthropic's evaluation guidance stresses defining success criteria that are *specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant*. For a business user this means deciding, ideally before you prompt, what a passing answer must contain: which questions it must resolve, which sources it must respect, what format it must take. Vague standards ("make it good") produce vague evaluation. Concrete criteria ("covers all four risk categories, cites the policy section for each, fits on one page") let you judge accuracy and completeness objectively and consistently.

- **Checking accuracy but forgetting completeness.** Evaluators often fact-check individual sentences while missing that a whole requested deliverable is absent. Always reconcile the output against the full ask.

# Identify Hallucinations, Inconsistencies, and Biases in Responses

This topic sits at the center of the exam's heaviest domain because it tests a specific professional skill: recognizing *how* an AI output can be wrong even when it looks right. Knowing the failure modes — fabrication, contradiction, and bias — is what lets you catch a problem before it reaches a customer, a regulator, or a decision-maker.


##### What a hallucination is

A hallucination is text that is factually incorrect or unsupported by the provided context, produced confidently as if it were true. Language models generate fluent, plausible language; fluency is not the same as accuracy. Anthropic states plainly that even advanced models like Claude can sometimes generate content that is factually wrong or inconsistent with the given context, and that techniques reduce but do not eliminate this.

- **Quotes** — words placed in quotation marks that the source never contains.
- **Statistics and figures** — a confident "37% increase" with no basis in the provided data.

concepts.summary: A model's expressed confidence (e.g., 'definitely') should not be treated as evidence of correctness; verification against an authoritative source is the only reliable signal.

grounding.text:
##### Self-reported confidence is not a reliability signal

This is one of the exam's clearest lessons. If Claude says "I'm confident," "definitely," or "I'm certain," that expression carries no evidentiary weight — a model can be equally fluent whether it is right or wrong, and it can be confidently wrong. Do not use the tone of certainty, or Claude's stated confidence level, as a proxy for correctness. Verification against an authoritative source is the only signal that counts. The tempting-but-wrong exam answer is "Claude said it was sure, so it's reliable"; the correct answer is "confidence is not verification — check it."


##### How to surface these problems

- **Trace every specific to a source.** Citations, numbers, and quotes should point to something real; if you can't confirm it, treat it as unverified.
- **Ask Claude to support each claim with a quote, and retract claims it can't support.** This makes fabrication visible.
- **Give permission to say "I don't know."** Uncertainty admitted is far safer than a gap filled with invention.

- **Re-run and compare.** Divergent answers to the same question flag instability.
- **Interrogate framing.** Ask "what's the strongest case against this?" to counter framing bias you may have introduced.

grounding.text:
# Apply Fact-Checking and Validation Techniques

Spotting that an output *might* be wrong is only half the skill; the exam's heaviest domain also tests whether you know the concrete techniques to *confirm* whether it is right. This topic is the practical toolkit: verifying against authoritative sources, cross-checking, using citations and connectors, and spot-checking quantitative results.


##### Verify against authoritative sources

The default validation move is to compare a claim against a trustworthy, independent source of truth — the original contract, the official statistic, the primary document, the system of record. "Authoritative" means the source that would settle the question in a dispute, not a convenient echo of the claim. Two principles matter:

- **Prefer primary over secondary.** Check the actual policy text, not a paraphrase of it. Anthropic's own hallucination guidance recommends having Claude work from provided documents and grounding claims in the real wording rather than general recall.
- **Match the source to the stakes.** A low-stakes internal note may need only a quick sanity check; a customer-facing or regulated claim needs the definitive source.


##### Cross-checking

Cross-checking validates a claim by confirming it from more than one independent angle. Techniques include:

- **Multiple sources.** Confirm a figure in two independent places; agreement raises confidence, disagreement flags a problem.
- **Best-of-N / regeneration.** Anthropic suggest

concepts.summary: When reviewing numerical data, one must recompute samples, sanity-check magnitudes, verify units and time frames, and trace every figure back to the underlying source data.

grounding.text:
##### Spot-check quantitative output

Numbers deserve special discipline because they look objective and are easy to fabricate.

- **Recompute a sample.** Re-add a column, re-derive a percentage, check that parts sum to the whole.
- **Sanity-check magnitude.** Does the number pass a "could this even be true?" test against what you know? A "220% market share" is impossible on its face.
- **Check units and time frames.** Confusions between thousands and millions, or monthly and annual, are common and consequential.
- **Trace figures to the data.** Every number in a summary should map to a value in the underlying source. If it doesn't appear there, treat it as invented until proven otherwise.

A worked example: Claude produces a budget table whose category lines total $480k but whose stated grand total is $500k. The internal mismatch is immediate evidence of an error; you recompute, find the true total, and do not forward the table until it reconciles.

- **Treating a citation or a confident tone as verification.** Neither is. Open the source; confidence is not a reliability signal.

- **Confusing consistency with truth.** Repeated agreement across regenerations can still be uniformly wrong; anchor at least one check to an authoritative source.

concepts.title: Risk-Based Triage in AI Usage
concepts.summary: Verification effort when using AI outputs must scale with the potential consequences of being wrong, requiring different levels of scrutiny for different tasks.

grounding.text:
# Determine When Human Review or Additional Verification Is Required

Not every Claude output needs the same scrutiny. The skill the exam tests here is *risk-based triage*: recognizing which outputs you can act on with a light check and which ones require a qualified human to review before anything is finalized or sent. Getting this judgment right is central to using Claude responsibly in a business setting.


##### The core principle: match verification to stakes

Verification effort should scale with the consequences of being wrong. A brainstormed list of blog-title ideas carries almost no risk if one is weak — quick self-review is enough. A benefits-eligibility determination, a contract clause, or a medical instruction carries serious risk if it is wrong — it demands human review by someone qualified, plus independent verification of the facts.

Anthropic's usage policy makes this concrete. For high-risk uses — including legal, financial, and employment decisions that affect people — it calls for additional safeguards such as **human-in-the-loop oversight**. Its guidance is that when Claude is used to provide advice, recommendations, or subjective decisions that directly affect individuals or consumers, **a qualified professional in that field must review the content or decision before it is disseminated or finalized**. And more broadly: keep a human in the loop for any consequential or irreversible decision, and treat model output as an input to your reasoning, not a repl

concepts.title: Meaningful Human Review
concepts.summary: Meaningful review requires a competent person to examine the substance, facts, and reasoning of an output, possessing the authority and time to change or reject it, rather than just rubber-stamping it.

grounding.text:
##### Human review is a control, not a courtesy

The exam distinguishes real oversight from theater. Meaningful review means a competent person actually examines the substance — checks the facts, the reasoning, and the fit — and has the authority and time to change or reject the output. A rubber-stamp ("looked fine, approved") is not the control the policy intends. Similarly, "additional verification" means an *independent* check against authoritative sources, not asking Claude whether it is sure. The model's self-reported confidence is not a reliability signal and never a substitute for human judgment on a high-stakes item.


##### A related control: handle sensitive data before use, not after

Escalation is not only about reviewing outputs; it is also about not creating avoidable risk on the way in. Before uploading regulated or confidential personal data, redact or anonymize it. Instructing Claude "don't retain this" is not a substitute for a real data control — the safeguard is what you do to the data, governed by your organization's policy, not a request to the model. When a task would require exposing sensitive data you're not authorized to share, that itself is a trigger to escalate to the appropriate owner rather than proceed.


##### Common pitfalls the exam tests

- **Treating a fluent, confident output as review-complete.** Polish and confidence are not verification; consequential items still need a qualified human.
- **Applying heavy review everywhere, or nowhere.

concepts.title: Data Handling Controls

##### Human review is a control, not a courtesy

The exam distinguishes real oversight from theater. Meaningful review means a competent person actually examines the substance — checks the facts, the reasoning, and the fit — and has the authority and time to change or reject the output. A rubber-stamp ("looked fine, approved") is not the control the policy intends. Similarly, "additional verification" means an *independent* check against authoritative sources, not asking Claude whether it is sure. The model's self-reported confidence is not a reliability signal and never a substitute for human judgment on a high-stakes item.


##### A related control: handle sensitive data before use, not after

Escalation is not only about reviewing outputs; it is also about not creating avoidable risk on the way in. Before uploading regulated or confidential personal data, redact or anonymize it. Instructing Claude "don't retain this" is not a substitute for a real data control — the safeguard is what you do to the data, governed by your organization's policy, not a request to the model. When a task would require exposing sensitive data you're not authorized to share, that itself is a trigger to escalate to the appropriate owner rather than proceed.


##### Common pitfalls the exam tests

- **Treating a fluent, confident output as review-complete.** Polish and confidence are not verification; consequential items still need a qualified human.
- **Applying heavy review everywhere, or nowhere.

grounding.text:
# Edit, Adapt, Refine, and Compare Outputs for the Intended Audience

A verified, accurate output is still not finished if it doesn't fit the person who will read it. This topic tests a working professional's craft: taking a correct first draft and shaping it — tone, level, length, format — for a specific audience, then iterating and comparing variants until it's right. On the exam it pairs naturally with evaluation: you verify that an output is *true*, then refine it so it is *usable*.


##### Start from the audience, not the draft

Before editing a word, define who will read this and what they need. The same underlying facts should be expressed very differently for different readers:

- **Executive / decision-maker:** lead with the recommendation and the "so what," keep it short, minimize jargon, surface risks and trade-offs.
- **Technical specialist / peer:** precision, detail, and correct terminology matter more than brevity.
- **Customer / external audience:** plain language, warm and on-brand tone, no internal shorthand, nothing unverified.
- **General or non-expert reader:** define terms, use analogies, shorter sentences.

The dimensions you adapt are consistent: **tone** (formal, friendly, authoritative), **reading level and jargon**, **length and depth**, **structure and format** (email, memo, bullet brief, table, slide outline), and **emphasis** (what leads, what's cut). The most common miss is a technically correct output pitched at the wrong altitude — accurate, b

concepts.title: Audience Adaptation in Communication
concepts.summary: Adapting a single set of facts into multiple outputs for different audiences requires careful rewriting of form while preserving the underlying truth.

grounding.text:
##### Worked mini-example

You have an accurate internal analysis of why a project slipped. For the **project team**, you refine it into a detailed retrospective with root causes and action items. For the **VP**, you ask Claude to compress the same content into a five-line update: status, impact, cause, fix, date. For the **client**, you adapt it again into a brief, reassuring note that omits internal blame and commits to next steps. One verified set of facts, three audience-shaped outputs. Editing does not change the truth; it changes the delivery — and you re-verify that no adaptation introduced a new unsupported claim.


##### Refinement must preserve accuracy

Editing for audience can quietly break correctness: shortening may drop a necessary caveat; simplifying may overstate a nuanced finding; a punchier tone may turn a hedge into a promise. After each refinement, re-check that the adapted version is still faithful to the verified facts and still complete for the ask. Adaptation is a rewrite of *form*, and every rewrite is a chance for a new error to enter.

Tools help here. **Artifacts** are well suited to content you'll iterate on — a document or brief in a side panel you can revise across turns while the chat stays a workspace. **Projects** let you store audience context, brand voice, and style guidelines as custom instructions and knowledge, so Claude adapts consistently to your standing audiences without re-explaining each time.

concepts.title: Output Format Selection
concepts.summary: Choosing the right container (Inline chat, Artifacts, or Structured/tabular) depends on how the reader intends to use the output.

grounding.text:
# Organize and Curate Information and Select Appropriate Output Formats

An output that is accurate and audience-appropriate can still fail if it arrives in the wrong container — a decision table buried in a wall of chat prose, or a quick answer over-engineered into a standalone document. This topic tests a practical judgment: how to organize and curate what Claude produces, and how to choose among Artifacts, inline chat, and structured/tabular formats so the information is usable.


##### Match the format to how the output will be used

Ask what the reader will *do* with the output. That answer picks the format.

- **Inline chat** is right for conversational, transient exchanges: quick answers, explanations, brainstorming, iterating on an idea, short responses you'll read once and move past. Chat is the workspace where you think out loud.
- **Artifacts** are right for substantial, self-contained content you'll want to keep, edit, reuse, or refer back to: a one-page brief, a policy draft, a project plan, a chart, a small interactive tool, a piece of code, a diagram. Anthropic describes Artifacts as standalone content shown in a dedicated side panel, typically generated when the content is significant (roughly fifteen-plus lines) and something you're likely to revise or reuse. The chat stays a conversation; the Artifact becomes the deliverable you iterate on.
- **Structured / tabular output** is right when information has repeating fields or must be compared across dimensions:

concepts.title: Inline Chat Usage
concepts.summary: Inline chat is best suited for quick, transient interactions like brainstorming, short answers, or iterative conversations.

concepts.summary: Claude offers several features—Projects, Memory, and Research mode/connectors—to organize information beyond a single chat response.

grounding.text:
##### Use the right feature to organize at scale

Beyond a single response, Claude's product features help organize information across a body of work:

- **Projects** hold custom instructions plus uploaded knowledge sources and can be shared within a team, so related conversations draw on a consistent, curated context — useful when many outputs must follow one standard or reference one set of documents.
- **Memory** persists relevant context across conversations, reducing repetition and keeping outputs consistent with what you've established.
- **Research mode and connectors** gather and organize information from the web and your own documents, returning cited results you can then shape into the right format.

Choosing where information lives — a passing chat, a durable Artifact, a Project's knowledge base — is itself an act of organization the exam expects you to reason about.


##### Decision rules to remember

- **Will they edit, reuse, or refer back to it, and is it substantial?** → Artifact.
- **Is it a quick, one-off answer or an idea in progress?** → Inline chat.
- **Does it have repeating fields or need side-by-side comparison?** → Table or structured list.
- **Does it need to be consistent across many conversations or shared with a team?** → Project (and let Memory carry context).

concepts.title: Claude Product Modes Overview
concepts.summary: Claude offers several distinct working modes—Chat, Projects, Research mode, and Artifacts—each suited for different types of tasks.

grounding.text:
# Select Appropriate Claude Product Features (Projects, Research Mode, Chat, Artifacts)

Claude is not a single box. The claude.ai product bundles several distinct working modes, and the exam tests whether you can match a business task to the right one. Choosing well saves time, keeps context organized, and produces outputs your colleagues can actually use; choosing poorly means re-pasting the same background into every conversation or letting a good draft get buried in chat scrollback.


##### The four features at a glance

Think of these as answering four different questions:

- **Chat** — "I have a one-off question or a quick task." A regular conversation, no special setup.
- **Projects** — "I do the same kind of work repeatedly, over the same materials." A persistent workspace with reusable instructions and a shared knowledge base.
- **Research mode** — "I need a thorough, cited answer that pulls from many sources." An agentic mode that runs many searches and returns a structured report with inline citations.
- **Artifacts** — "I want a standalone piece of content I can see, edit, and reuse." A side-panel document, diagram, or mini-app separate from the chat text.

They are not mutually exclusive. You can produce an Artifact inside a Project, or turn on Research mode within a chat. The skill is knowing which one leads.

##### Research mode: thorough, cited, multi-source answers

Research mode makes Claude work **agentically**: it launches broad searches, spins up sub-agents to investigate different angles concurrently, and progressively narrows its focus, then returns a structured report with **inline numerical citations** linking to the sources it used. It trades speed for depth — answers take minutes rather than seconds — and is available on paid plans.

Use Research mode when the answer must be comprehensive and verifiable: competitive landscape scans, literature-style reviews, market or vendor comparisons, or any question where you will need to check the sources. The citations are the point — they let you verify claims rather than trust them. That matters because Claude can produce specific-looking but fabricated details; a cited report gives you links to confirm before you rely on the findings. Do not use Research mode for a quick factual lookup or a creative draft — it is slower and heavier than the task needs.

grounding.text:
# Differentiate Between Claude Model Types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)

Anthropic offers Claude in a family of model tiers, not a single model. The exam expects you to know the three headline tiers — **Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus** — and, more importantly, what each is *for*. The names are consistent across generations: a tier tells you the tradeoff between speed and cost on one side and raw capability on the other. Knowing the tier framing lets you pick sensibly without memorizing version numbers.


##### The core idea: a speed/cost vs. capability spectrum

Picture a straight line. On one end sits **Haiku** — the fastest and cheapest. On the other end sits **Opus** — the most capable and the slowest and most expensive. **Sonnet** sits in the middle as the balanced default. Every model in the family lands somewhere on that spectrum, and moving toward more capability costs you speed and money, while moving toward more speed and lower cost costs you some depth of reasoning.

The important exam insight is that "more capable" is not universally "better." A model that is overkill for the task wastes latency and budget; a model that is underpowered produces work you cannot use. The right answer is the tier that *matches the task*, which is why the exam frames model choice as a tradeoff rather than a ranking.

##### A note on the wider family

Anthropic also offers **Fable 5** as an even more capable frontier model that sits above Opus. It is worth knowing it exists, but the exam blueprint frames model selection around the three named tiers — Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus — so anchor your thinking on those three. When a question asks you to choose among model *types*, it is testing the Haiku/Sonnet/Opus tradeoff.


##### Putting it together: a quick mental table

- **Simple, fast, high-volume, cheap** → Haiku.
- **Balanced, general-purpose, most everyday and production work** → Sonnet (the default).
- **Hardest reasoning, complex/long-horizon, quality over cost** → Opus.

- **Treating Opus as the "right" answer by default.** "Use the most capable model" is a tempting but usually wrong choice. For simple, high-volume tasks it wastes cost and latency; the correct answer matches a cheaper, faster tier to the work.

# Align Model Selection With Task Requirements (Cost, Speed, Quality)

Knowing the Claude tiers exists is only half the skill. The exam wants you to *decide* — to look at a real task and pick the tier that fits its actual requirements. This is a business-judgment call balancing three levers: **cost, speed, and quality.** The single most tested lesson in this domain is that the best model is the one that matches the task, not the most powerful one you can access.


##### The three levers you are trading off

Every task pulls on three constraints at once:

- **Cost** — you pay per unit of work. On high-volume tasks, small per-item differences multiply into large bills.
- **Speed (latency)** — how long each response takes. When a person or a downstream process is waiting, latency is part of the user experience, not just an efficiency metric.
- **Quality** — how good, deep, and reliable the output needs to be for its purpose.

You cannot maximize all three. More capability (quality) generally means more cost and more latency. The art is deciding how much quality the task genuinely requires, then buying exactly that much — no more.

grounding.text:
# Understand and Manage Context Limitations and Memory Considerations

Claude reads and reasons over a **context window** — the working memory of a single conversation. It is large but finite, and how you manage it directly affects the quality of Claude's answers. The exam tests whether you recognize the signs that a conversation has outgrown its context and know the right corrective move: restart, summarize, or persist. This is practical hygiene that separates smooth Claude use from frustrating, drifting sessions.


##### What the context window is

Everything in an active conversation — your messages, Claude's replies, and any documents you paste or upload — shares one finite budget of "context." As a chat grows longer, that budget fills up. Claude does not have unlimited recall of the whole conversation forever; it works within the window available to it. A Project, for comparison, provides a large dedicated context (on the order of a 500-page book) for its knowledge base, and can extend capacity further when that knowledge approaches the limit. But any single ongoing chat still operates within a bounded window.

The key mental model: context is a **desk, not a filing cabinet.** Only so much fits on the desk at once. When it overflows, the earliest items effectively get pushed off, and things you said long ago can lose influence over the current answer.

concepts.title: Context Persistence Mechanisms
concepts.summary: Context can be persisted deliberately beyond a single conversation using Projects or Memory to ensure continuity.

grounding.text:
##### When to persist (Projects and Memory)

When context needs to survive *beyond* a single conversation, don't rely on chat history — persist it deliberately:

- **Projects** are the durable home for reusable context. Put the stable reference documents, instructions, tone, and role into a Project's custom instructions and knowledge base once. Every new chat in that Project starts already grounded, so you never re-paste the background. Each Project also keeps its own focused summary and memory space, separate from other Projects and from ordinary chats.
- **Memory** lets Claude carry context and details about you across standalone conversations. Claude can build a synthesis of key insights from your chat history and use it to provide continuity in new conversations, so you are not reintroducing yourself each time. Memory can be managed and paused in settings, and Project memory is kept separate from general chat memory.

Rule of thumb: **within one task, summarize; across many tasks over time, persist in a Project; for personal continuity across conversations, rely on Memory.**

- **A 60-message brainstorm that has wandered.** Claude is repeating itself and forgot an early constraint. → Ask for a summary of decisions and constraints, then **restart** in a fresh chat with that summary.

# Apply Claude to Analyze Requirements and Use Cases

Before Claude drafts a single deliverable, the more valuable work is often earlier: turning a vague business goal into a clear, testable set of requirements, and honestly judging whether an AI assistant is even the right tool. This topic tests whether you can use Claude as a thinking partner for scoping — and whether you can tell a good AI fit from a bad one.

Most real requests arrive underspecified: "Help us improve onboarding," "We need a better weekly report," "Can AI handle our support inbox?" A strong practitioner does not immediately ask Claude to produce output. They first use Claude to *interrogate the request*.

A reliable move is to ask Claude to act as a business analyst and generate clarifying questions before proposing anything: "I want to redesign our customer onboarding email sequence. Before you draft anything, ask me the 8–10 questions you'd need answered to scope this well." concepts.title: Good AI Fit Criteria
concepts.summary: A task is a good fit for AI when it involves language, synthesis, drafting, or reasoning over supplied text, and a knowledgeable human can verify the output.

grounding.text:
##### Assessing whether a task is a good AI fit

The exam explicitly rewards the judgment of *when not to use AI, or where to keep a human in the loop*. A task is generally a **good fit** for Claude when it involves language, synthesis, drafting, transformation, or reasoning over text you can supply, AND a knowledgeable human can verify the output. Strong-fit examples: summarizing long documents, drafting first-pass content, restructuring notes, comparing options, generating test data, explaining a concept, converting a format.

A task is a **poor or high-risk fit** when it has one or more of these traits:

- **It needs a single, authoritative, checkable fact and no one will verify it.** Because models can fabricate specific-looking details — citations, statute subsection numbers, figures — an unverified factual lookup for a compliance or legal audience is a bad fit. The output *looks* trustworthy, which is exactly the danger. Self-reported confidence ("I'm certain the regulation says X") is not a reliability signal.
- **It depends on private, regulated, or personal data that hasn't been handled correctly.** If the use case requires uploading customer PII, health, or financial records, the data-sensitivity control comes *first*: redact or anonymize before uploading, and confirm the workspace's data terms. Telling Claude "don't remember this" is not a substitute for a real policy control.
- **The decision has legal, safety, financial, or ethical weight and would be executed au

concepts.title: Poor or High-Risk AI Fit Traits
concepts.summary: Tasks are poor fits if they require unverified authoritative facts, involve sensitive private data, require automatic execution of high-stakes decisions, or need real-time system access Claude lacks.

concepts.title: Claude Research Mode
concepts.summary: Claude's research mode is agentic, meaning it plans inquiries, runs multiple searches, and returns synthesized answers with verifiable inline citations.

grounding.text:
# Leverage Claude for Research, Planning, and Process Optimization

Knowledge workers spend a large share of their time gathering information, planning work, and looking for ways to make repeatable processes faster. This topic tests whether you can direct Claude — including its agentic research mode — to do that gathering and planning well, and, critically, whether you verify what it returns before acting on it.


##### Research: using research mode well

Claude's **research mode** is agentic: instead of a single search, it plans a line of inquiry, runs multiple searches that build on each other, decides what to investigate next, and returns a synthesized answer with **inline citations you can click to verify**. When connectors are enabled, it can research across both the public web and your internal context (for example Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Docs), so a single query can pull together external market data and your own meeting notes. Research is available on paid plans and is turned on from the "+" menu in the chat; a common failure is expecting deep research from a plain chat — if Claude doesn't do it automatically, explicitly ask it to "use the research tool."

Good practice with research mode:

- **Scope the question.** "Research the top three project-management tools for a 20-person agency, comparing price, integrations, and onboarding effort, and cite each claim" beats "tell me about PM tools." A scoped question produces checkable, comparable output.
- **Ask

concepts.title: Effective Prompting for Planning
concepts.summary: Effective prompts for planning should provide Claude with a specific role, a clear goal, defined constraints, and a desired output format.

grounding.text:
##### Planning: turning goals into a workable plan

Claude is strong at converting an objective into a structured plan you can critique. Effective prompts give it a role, the goal, the constraints, and the output shape: "You are a program manager. Draft a 6-week plan to migrate our team to a new ticketing system. Assume 4 people at 20% time. Produce phases, milestones, dependencies, risks, and an owner column."

High-value planning patterns:

- **Work backward from the deadline.** Ask Claude to start from the target date and derive what must be true each week. This surfaces schedule conflicts early.
- **Pressure-test the plan.** "Play devil's advocate: where is this plan most likely to slip, and what's the single biggest risk I'm underweighting?" A second pass as a skeptic catches optimism that the first draft baked in.
- **Generate options, not just an answer.** For a decision, ask for two or three approaches with explicit tradeoffs rather than one recommendation. You stay the decision-maker; Claude widens the option set.
- **Iterate in a Project.** For multi-week planning, keep the plan and its source documents in a Project so context persists and teammates work from the same version instead of re-explaining the situation each session.

Remember that Claude does not know your unstated constraints — budget ceilings, politics, a fixed vendor. State them, or the plan will be plausible but inapplicable.


##### Process optimization: finding improvements

Claude is a useful lens

# Use Claude to Support Solution Design, Development, and Iteration

Once requirements are clear, Claude helps you move from idea to a working deliverable — a document, a template, a dashboard mock-up, a small interactive tool — and then refine it through fast cycles of feedback. This topic tests whether you can drive that build-and-iterate loop deliberately, using the right features, rather than accepting the first draft.


##### Drafting the first solution

The fastest way to a good deliverable is a good first draft to react to. Claude produces one quickly when you give it four things: a **role** ("you are a UX writer"), the **goal**, the **constraints** (audience, length, tone, format, what to avoid), and an **example or template** if you have one. "Draft a one-page project brief for a website redesign; audience is non-technical executives; under 400 words; include goals, scope, timeline, and risks" yields something you can immediately critique.

A first draft is a starting point, not the deliverable. The exam favors the practitioner who treats Claude's output as raw material to be verified and shaped, not as a finished answer. Any factual claim in the draft — a statistic, a date, a cited source — is unverified until you check it, because models can produce specific-looking details that are wrong.

concepts.title: Effective Iteration Strategies
concepts.summary: Effective iteration requires providing specific, targeted feedback, making changes in small, manageable steps, and using Claude to critique its own work.

grounding.text:
##### Iterating toward the deliverable

Iteration is where Claude adds the most value, and doing it well is a skill the exam probes. Effective iteration is *specific and one change at a time*.

- **Give targeted feedback.** "Tighten paragraph two, cut the jargon, and make the call-to-action more direct" beats "make it better." Vague feedback produces a random rewrite; specific feedback converges.
- **Iterate in small steps.** Change one dimension per pass so you can tell what improved. Sweeping "redo everything" prompts make it hard to keep the parts that were already good.
- **Have Claude critique its own work.** "Review this draft as a skeptical stakeholder and list its three weakest points" surfaces problems before a real reviewer does — but treat the critique as input, not gospel.
- **Preserve good versions.** When a version is close, save it before the next change so an experiment can't lose progress.
- **Anchor with examples.** Pasting a "good" example and a "bad" example teaches Claude your standard faster than adjectives do.

Use a **Project** to hold the deliverable, its source material, and a custom instruction ("our brand voice is plain, confident, no hype") so every iteration stays consistent and a teammate can pick up where you left off. **Memory** can carry preferences across conversations so you re-state them less, though you should still confirm important constraints rather than assume they carried over.

concepts.summary: Adopting AI like Claude involves two main strategies: augmenting an existing workflow by inserting AI into steps, or redesigning the entire workflow because AI enables a fundamentally different process shape.

grounding.text:
# Integrate Claude into Existing Workflows to Augment or Redesign Them

The goal of adopting Claude is rarely "use AI"; it's to make an existing workflow faster, more consistent, or higher quality. This topic tests whether you can decide *where* Claude belongs in a real process, whether to **augment** the current flow or **redesign** it, and how to keep the right human checkpoints so the result is trustworthy.


##### Augment versus redesign

There are two fundamentally different integration strategies, and choosing correctly is a core judgment the exam probes.

**Augment** means keeping the workflow's shape and inserting Claude into specific steps to make them faster or better. The process, roles, and hand-offs stay the same; Claude drafts, summarizes, triages, or checks within them. This is lower-risk, quick to adopt, and reversible. Example: a support team keeps its existing ticket queue and reviewer, but Claude now drafts the first-pass reply for the agent to edit and send.

**Redesign** means rethinking the workflow because AI makes a fundamentally different shape possible. Steps get removed, merged, or reordered; the human role shifts from *doing* to *reviewing*. This unlocks bigger gains but carries more change-management and risk. Example: instead of a monthly report assembled by hand, a team builds a repeatable Project where Claude drafts the whole narrative from supplied data, and the analyst's job becomes verifying and approving rather than writing.

concepts.title: Human-in-the-loop (HITL)
concepts.summary: HITL requires a human to review or approve AI-influenced output before it has a real-world effect, with the required level of review depending on the stakes of the task.

grounding.text:
##### Human-in-the-loop: the non-negotiable

The exam consistently rewards keeping a human checkpoint where it matters. "Human-in-the-loop" means a person reviews or approves before an AI-influenced output has real-world effect. Where to place the checkpoint depends on stakes:

- **High stakes** (legal, financial, medical, HR, anything customer-facing and irreversible, anything for a compliance audience): mandatory human review before release. Because Claude can produce specific-looking but fabricated details, and its confident tone is not a reliability signal, the reviewer verifies the load-bearing facts against an authoritative source.
- **Medium stakes** (internal drafts, routine external replies): lighter review, perhaps spot-checks.
- **Low stakes, high volume** (tagging, routing, first-draft summaries seen only internally): a person can supervise in aggregate rather than checking each item.

Design the checkpoint into the workflow explicitly — "agent edits and approves every reply before it sends" — rather than hoping someone catches errors. A workflow that lets unreviewed AI output reach customers or regulators is a design flaw, not a speed feature.

concepts.summary: When presenting AI value to stakeholders, frame benefits in concrete business terms like time saved or quality improvement, rather than using vague hype.

grounding.text:
# Communicate Claude's Value and Limitations to Stakeholders

Getting value from Claude in an organization depends as much on how you talk about it as on how you use it. This topic tests whether you can make an honest case for Claude — real benefits *and* real limits — set expectations that survive contact with reality, and tell stakeholders exactly where human oversight and escalation are required.


##### Articulating the value honestly

Stakeholders (a manager, a client, a review board) want to know what they'll get. Frame value in *business terms*, not features: time saved, faster turnaround, more consistent quality, wider option-generation, fewer routine handoffs. Concrete framing lands better than hype: "Claude drafts the first version of our weekly report in minutes, so the analyst spends their time verifying and interpreting instead of assembling" is more credible than "AI will transform our reporting."

Ground the value in what Claude genuinely does well: summarizing and synthesizing long documents, drafting and rewriting content, structuring messy information, comparing options, researching across many sources with citations, and prototyping tangible deliverables like dashboards and templates through Artifacts. Anthropic positions Claude as a productivity layer for knowledge work, and the honest pitch stays inside that lane.

The tempting mistake is to oversell — "it's basically an autonomous employee," "it's always right," "we can fire the review step." Overselling

concepts.summary: When implementing AI tools, it is crucial to translate abstract value into concrete, measurable expectations for stakeholders.

grounding.text:
##### Setting expectations that hold up

Translate value and limits into concrete expectations:

- **Show the human's role.** Make clear that a person reviews and verifies before anything high-stakes ships. Stakeholders trust "Claude drafts, a named human approves" far more than "the AI handles it."
- **Define what "good" looks like.** Tie expectations to checkable acceptance criteria ("summaries under 200 words, every figure traceable to the source") so success isn't subjective.
- **Frame it as a fast draft-and-verify loop**, not a magic answer button. This primes stakeholders to expect iteration and a verification step rather than instant perfection.
- **Right-size the tooling story.** If cost or speed is a stakeholder concern, explain that the model tier is matched to the task — a faster, cheaper tier for simple high-volume steps, a more capable tier reserved for genuinely complex work — so they hear cost-discipline, not "always use the biggest model."

# Configure Claude Projects with Instructions and Knowledge Sources

A **Project** in claude.ai is a dedicated workspace that bundles reusable *custom instructions* and a persistent *knowledge base* so that every conversation inside it starts with the same context. On the Foundations exam, this topic tests whether you understand how to set up a Project correctly, how uploaded knowledge and instructions shape Claude's answers, and how to share a Project with a team without leaking permissions or stale information.


##### What a Project is and why it matters

A regular chat is stateless: each new conversation begins with a blank slate, so you re-paste the same background material and re-explain the same rules every time. A Project fixes that. You create it once, give it a name and description, write instructions that apply to all chats inside it, and attach the reference documents Claude should draw on. From then on, every conversation you (or a teammate) start within that Project inherits that setup automatically.

Projects are available to everyone, including free accounts, which can create up to five. To create one, go to claude.ai/projects, click **+ New Project**, and provide a name and description. The description is not decorative — it is a lightweight signal of the Project's purpose and helps teammates find the right workspace.


##### Setting custom instructions

Custom instructions are standing guidance that Claude reads before responding in any chat within the Proje

concepts.title: Project Knowledge Base Management
concepts.summary: The knowledge base is where users upload documents, text files, and code snippets to be used across all chats within a project. Uploaded content is persistent across the project.

grounding.text:
##### Adding knowledge sources

The **knowledge base** appears on the right side of the Project's main page. Click the **+** button to upload documents, text files, and code snippets. As Anthropic's documentation puts it, "anything you upload to this space will be used across all of your chats within that project." This is the difference between attaching a file to one chat (visible only there) and adding it to Project knowledge (visible to every chat in the Project, persistently).

Practical limits matter here. Project files are capped at **30 MB per file**, with no fixed count limit — but the total content must fit within Claude's working capacity. Supported formats include PDF, DOCX, CSV, TXT, and more. For most non-PDF files Claude extracts text only, so a scanned image embedded in a Word document will not be "read."

**RAG mode.** On paid plans, when your project knowledge grows large enough to approach the context-window limit, Claude automatically switches on **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** mode. Instead of loading every document in full, Claude retrieves the most relevant passages for each question. This expands how much knowledge a Project can hold, but it changes behavior subtly: Claude sees excerpts, not the whole corpus at once, so precise, well-labeled documents retrieve better than one enormous catch-all file. A common exam-style pitfall is assuming a huge knowledge base guarantees Claude "has read everything" — under RAG it retrieves selectively, and p

concepts.title: Data Sensitivity and Privacy
concepts.summary: Sensitive data must be protected by applying data-sensitivity controls before uploading it, as simple instructions to the AI are insufficient for real privacy.

grounding.text:
##### Common pitfalls the exam rewards you for avoiding

- **Putting sensitive data in the wrong place.** Apply data-sensitivity controls *before* uploading. Redact or anonymize regulated personal data first; instructing Claude "don't retain this" is not a substitute for a real privacy control.
- **Confusing chat attachments with Project knowledge.** A file added to one chat does not carry across the Project. Upload it to the knowledge base if it should persist.
- **Letting knowledge go stale.** Instructions and files reflect the moment they were written; a Project that is never reviewed will confidently answer from outdated material.


##### Sources

- [How can I create and manage projects? — Anthropic Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177-how-can-i-create-and-manage-projects)
- [Understanding Claude's Personalization Features — Anthropic Help Center](https://support.anthropic.com/en/articles/10185728-understanding-claude-s-personalization-features)
- [Upload files to Claude — Claude Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8241126-what-kinds-of-documents-can-i-upload-to-claude-ai)
- [Use Google Workspace connectors — Claude Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10166901-using-the-google-drive-integration)

concepts.title: Knowledge Sources for Claude
concepts.summary: Claude can utilize two primary sources of external knowledge: static uploaded files or live data accessed via connectors.

grounding.text:
# Manage Uploaded Knowledge and Connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)

Claude can draw on two kinds of external knowledge: **files you upload** and **connectors** that link Claude to live services like Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Calendar. This topic tests your judgment about *what to connect, what permissions that grants, how the data is accessed, and how to keep sources relevant* — the everyday governance a business user is responsible for.


##### Two ways to give Claude your knowledge

**Uploaded files** are static snapshots. You attach a document to a single chat or, more durably, to a Project's knowledge base, and Claude reads that copy. If the underlying document changes later, the uploaded copy does not — you must re-upload.

**Connectors** link Claude to a live source, so Claude reads the current state on demand. The Google Workspace connectors (Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar) are the ones the exam names explicitly. Google Docs added through the Drive connector "sync directly from Google Drive, so you're always working with the latest version" — a key advantage over a stale uploaded copy.

Choosing between them is a judgment call: upload a fixed reference (a signed contract, a finalized policy) so it cannot drift; connect a living source (an evolving planning doc, your inbox, your calendar) so Claude always sees current reality.


##### Managing uploaded files

Files can be added to an individual chat or to a Project's **Files** section for persistent reus

concepts.title: Connector Permissions and Scope
concepts.summary: Connectors operate strictly within the user's existing permissions and require explicit approval for every action taken on their behalf.

grounding.text:
##### Permissions, scope, and approval — the part the exam cares about

Several safeguards define what a connector can and cannot do, and they are exactly the kind of detail an exam question probes:

- **Claude mirrors your existing permissions.** You cannot use Claude to reach anything you couldn't already open yourself in Google Workspace. A connector does not escalate access.
- **Explicit approval per action.** Each action Claude takes on your behalf requires your approval. Claude does not silently rummage through your account.
- **Gmail is read-and-draft only — never send.** Claude only reads emails and creates drafts with your approval; the send function is not enabled, so every message must be sent manually from your own Gmail. During OAuth, Google's screen may mention send permissions, but Claude's behavior is restricted to reading and drafting. A tempting-but-wrong exam answer is "Claude can send the email for you" — it cannot; you send it.
- **Minimum necessary data.** Claude accesses your data only when a specific request requires it and retrieves the least it needs, rather than ingesting your whole account.
- **Citations.** Responses include citations showing which emails, events, or documents were used, with links to the originals where available — so you can verify the basis of an answer.


##### Data-access considerations and privacy discipline

Connector data is encrypted at rest and in transit, and information retrieved through a connector is retained alongsid

# Create Effective System-Level Instructions

System-level instructions — what claude.ai calls **profile instructions** (account-wide) and **project instructions** (per workspace) — are the standing guidance Claude reads before it responds. concepts.title: Instructions vs. Prompt Distinction
concepts.summary: Instructions should contain durable rules that apply across many conversations, while prompts should contain requests specific to a single, immediate task.

grounding.text:
##### What belongs in instructions vs. a single prompt

This is the distinction the exam is most likely to test. Put something in **instructions** when it is *durable* — true across many future conversations. Put it in a **prompt** when it is *specific to this one task*.

- Belongs in instructions: your role, your audience, your standing tone and format, your do-not rules, recurring context ("we operate in the EU, so assume GDPR applies").
- Belongs in the prompt: "Summarize *this* report in 200 words," "make *this* paragraph more formal," "draft a reply to *this* email."

A common mistake is stuffing a one-off request into the Project instructions ("summarize the Q3 deck"). It doesn't belong there — it will confuse every unrelated future chat in that Project. The reverse mistake is re-pasting your role and style rules into every prompt; that's exactly what instructions exist to eliminate. If you find yourself typing the same preamble repeatedly, promote it to instructions.


##### Keep instructions durable and lean

Instructions are read on *every* relevant conversation, so bloat has a cost: contradictory or excessive rules dilute the ones that matter. Favor a tight set of clear, high-value directives over an exhaustive list. When two instructions conflict, Claude has to guess — so keep them consistent and remove rules that no longer apply.

concepts.title: Configuration Decay Risk
concepts.summary: Claude configurations, including instructions and knowledge sources, are snapshots in time and can become outdated, leading to fluent but factually incorrect outputs.

grounding.text:
# Inform, Maintain, and Update Claude Configurations, Knowledge Sources, and Instructions

Setting up a Project, uploading knowledge, and writing instructions is a beginning, not an end. Configurations decay: documents are superseded, teammates change, policies are revised, and instructions written for last quarter quietly mislead this quarter. This topic tests whether you treat a Claude configuration as something that must be **owned, reviewed, and kept current** — and whether you recognize the general risk of stale configuration.


##### Why maintenance is a first-class concern

Every part of a Claude setup is a snapshot of the moment it was written. A Project instruction that says "our fiscal year ends in March" was true when typed and may be false after a reorganization. An uploaded pricing sheet reflects the day it was uploaded. A connector was authorized for a project that may have ended months ago. None of these self-correct. Claude will confidently answer from whatever is in front of it, so *stale configuration produces stale-but-confident output* — one of the more insidious failure modes because nothing looks broken. The output is fluent and internally consistent; it is just wrong because the source is old.

This is the core judgment the exam rewards: recognizing that "I set it up once" is not the same as "it is correct now," and building a habit of verifying live state before relying on it.

concepts.title: Connector and Access Management
concepts.summary: Connectors and sharing settings carry long-term data-access consequences, requiring periodic auditing of active connections and project permissions.

grounding.text:
##### Reviewing connectors and access

Connectors and sharing are configuration too, and they carry data-access consequences that outlast the work they were set up for:

- **Audit connector scope periodically.** A Drive or Gmail connection authorized for one project may still be active long after. Review what is connected; disconnect what is no longer needed via **Customize > Connectors**. Reducing standing access is good hygiene.
- **Review project membership and permissions.** On Team and Enterprise plans, revisit who has **Can use** versus **Can edit** on shared Projects. People change roles and leave teams; edit rights on a widely-trusted Project should be held by a small, current set of maintainers, not everyone who once needed access.
- **Re-check data sensitivity.** A source that was fine to include when the Project was internal may not be once the Project is shared more broadly. Apply sensitivity controls to the *current* audience, not the original one.


##### Ownership: the piece that makes maintenance actually happen

The most common real-world failure is diffuse responsibility: a shared Project that "everyone uses and no one maintains" degrades until people quietly stop trusting it. Assign a clear **owner** for each important configuration — a person accountable for keeping knowledge current, reviewing instructions, and managing access. Ownership is why the earlier advice to grant **Can edit** sparingly matters: a small maintainer group can keep a Project coherent
